articles.headline: Treasury Designates Iranian Oil Traders and Facilitators, Issues Cuba FAQs
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting Iranian oil traders and government-linked facilitators. These individuals and entities are accused of helping Tehran sell oil abroad and misappropriating the proceeds, as part of 'Operation Economic Outcast'.

The action was taken under two executive orders, one targeting Iran's petroleum, petrochemical, and aviation sectors, and another utilizing counterterrorism authorities. Among those sanctioned are Mohammad Javad Bavand, a former Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) intelligence officer, and Majid Taj, brother of the head of the Iranian Football Federation, who allegedly lead a network selling oil from Iran's dwindling reserves.
Separately, OFAC also issued new Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) related to Cuba sanctions. These FAQs provide guidance on the implementation of existing Cuba-related sanctions programs.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Illicit Drugs General License, Amends Russia-Related GL
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued Illicit Drugs General License (GL) 1, authorizing the wind down of transactions involving certain persons blocked on November 19, 2026. This new general license aims to provide a limited period for the orderly cessation of activities with newly designated individuals and entities involved in illicit drug trade.

In a separate but related action, OFAC also issued an amended Russia-related General License 131L. This amended license authorizes certain transactions for the negotiation of and entry into contingent contracts for the sale of Lukoil International GmbH and related maintenance activities.

Accompanying the amended Russia-related GL, OFAC also published two associated, amended Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs 1224 and 1225) to provide further clarity on the scope and application of the updated license.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new counter terrorism designations. These actions target individuals and entities deemed to be involved in supporting terrorist activities globally. The specific details of the designated parties were added to OFAC's Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List.

These designations are part of ongoing efforts by the U.S. government to disrupt the financial networks of terrorist organizations and their facilitators. The aim is to prevent these groups from accessing the international financial system and limit their ability to plan and carry out attacks.
Further information regarding the specific individuals and entities designated can be found on OFAC's website, which provides updated details on the SDN List.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Guatemalan Drug Trafficking Organizations with Terror Links
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations, targeting several Guatemalan drug trafficking organizations. These groups, including 'Los Lorenzana' (also known as the Lorenzana Drug Trafficking Organization) and 'Los Mendoza Drug Trafficking Organization', have been identified for their involvement in illicit drug trade and their support for Mexican narco-terrorist cartels.

The designations highlight the nexus between drug trafficking and terrorism, with OFAC noting that these organizations play a key role in moving cocaine between Colombia and Mexico, often working with groups like Mexico's Sinaloa Cartel.

These actions aim to disrupt the financial and operational capabilities of these transnational criminal organizations, preventing them from engaging in further illicit activities and undermining regional stability. The designations carry secondary sanctions risk under Executive Order 13224, as amended by Executive Order 13886.

articles.headline: OFAC Updates Iran Designation Listings
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced an update to its Iran designation listings. This action involves modifications to existing entries on the Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List related to Iran. These updates are part of OFAC's ongoing efforts to maintain the accuracy and effectiveness of its sanctions programs.

While specific details of the updates were not immediately released in a separate press statement, such actions typically involve adding new aliases, addresses, or other identifying information for already sanctioned individuals or entities, or making minor adjustments to existing entries.

These regular updates are crucial for financial institutions and other entities to ensure their compliance screening systems are current and accurately reflect the latest sanctions targets related to Iran.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Iran-Related Designations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations. These actions target individuals and entities involved in various illicit activities supporting the Iranian regime, including its petroleum, petrochemical, and aviation sectors.

These designations are part of a broader strategy to exert economic pressure on Iran, aiming to disrupt its ability to fund destabilizing activities in the region and develop its weapons programs. The Treasury Department has emphasized its commitment to denying Tehran access to revenue used for these purposes.

The specific details of the newly designated parties have been added to OFAC's Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List, requiring U.S. persons and entities to block their property and interests in property and generally prohibiting transactions with them.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Cyber and Transnational Criminal Organizations, Expands Cuba Sanctions
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting cyber-related threats and transnational criminal organizations. These actions aim to disrupt malicious cyber activities and the illicit financial networks supporting organized crime globally.

In a separate but significant move, OFAC also imposed new Cuba designations and published a Cuba-related determination. This determination expands the sector-based sanctions authority under Executive Order (E.O.) 14404 to include the electronics, manufacturing, marine, and technology sectors of the Cuban economy.

This expansion means that any foreign person determined by the State Department or Treasury to operate, or have operated, in these newly identified sectors of the Cuban economy is now exposed to blocking sanctions. This significantly broadens the scope of U.S. sanctions against the Cuban regime and those who enable it.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Iran-Related Designations, Alert on Shadow Fleet, and Amends Venezuela GL
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations and updates to certain Iran-related listings. These actions are part of 'Operation Economic Outcast' and target networks involved in global maritime fraud supporting the Iranian regime, as well as fraudulent ship registries and aviation support.

Concurrently, OFAC published an Iran-related Alert titled 'Iranian Shadow Fleet Reliance on False Flags for Sanctions Evasion'. This alert highlights the substantial risk of designation or penalties for providing services to vessels using false flags to circumvent U.S. sanctions on Iran.

Additionally, OFAC issued an amended Venezuela-related General License 5AA, 'Authorizing Certain Transactions Related to the Petróleos de Venezuela, S.A. 2020 8.5 Percent Bond on or After December 18, 2026,' along with an amended Frequently Asked Question (FAQ 595).

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the issuance of an amended Iran-related General License. This amendment modifies existing authorizations for certain transactions involving Iran, reflecting ongoing adjustments to U.S. sanctions policy.

General Licenses are issued by OFAC to authorize categories of transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under sanctions programs. Amendments can expand, narrow, or clarify the scope of permitted activities.
Entities engaged in Iran-related transactions are advised to review the amended General License carefully to ensure continued compliance with U.S. sanctions regulations.

articles.region: North Korea / Democratic Republic of the Congo
articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Designations on North Korea and Democratic Republic of the Congo
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting individuals and entities connected to North Korea. These actions are part of ongoing efforts to counter North Korea's weapons of mass destruction programs and other illicit activities.

In a separate action, OFAC also imposed designations related to the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). These designations aim to address issues of corruption, human rights abuses, and other destabilizing activities within the DRC.
The specific details of the designated parties have been added to OFAC's Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List, requiring U.S. persons and entities to comply with the associated prohibitions.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks, Inc. Settles with OFAC for $1,529,685
body: Extreme Networks, Inc., a U.S.-based networking company, has agreed to pay $1,529,685 to settle its potential civil liability for apparent violations of U.S. sanctions regulations. The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the settlement, which addresses transactions that contravened sanctions programs.

The specific details of the violations were outlined in OFAC's enforcement release, which typically includes information on the nature of the transactions, the sanctions programs involved, and the aggravating and mitigating factors considered in determining the penalty amount.

This enforcement action underscores the importance for companies, particularly those with international operations, to maintain robust sanctions compliance programs to prevent unauthorized dealings with sanctioned jurisdictions or individuals.

articles.headline: Bank of America, N.A. Pays $11,662,930 in OFAC Sanctions Settlement
body: Bank of America, N.A. has agreed to pay $11,662,930 to settle 475 apparent violations of various U.S. sanctions programs, as announced by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC). This settlement was part of a coordinated enforcement action by the U.S. Treasury Department, which also included significant penalties from FinCEN and the OCC for anti-money laundering failures.

The violations, which occurred between September 2021 and April 2025, involved transactions totaling approximately $14.8 million across sanctions programs related to Russia, Belarus, Iran, Burma, Somalia, narcotics, and global terrorism. OFAC identified issues such as delayed updates to screening filters, analyst errors, and alert suppression rules.

While OFAC deemed the violations non-egregious and mostly not voluntarily disclosed, the case highlights critical lessons for sanctions screening programs, including the need for accurate vendor data, timely filter updates, effective alert prioritization, and minimizing human error.

articles.headline: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics Settles with OFAC for $175,015 Over Sanctioned Supplier Deal
body: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics, a California-based freight forwarder, has agreed to pay $175,015 to settle apparent violations of OFAC's counter narcotics sanctions and reporting obligations. The violations stemmed from arranging the shipment of a sugar packet-filling machine from a sanctioned Chinese supplier, Youli Technology Development Co., Ltd.

OFAC found that Pegasus failed to adequately screen the supplier, even after Youli changed its name but retained its SDN-listed phone number and email address. The company also initially provided an incomplete response to an administrative subpoena from OFAC, which contributed significantly to the penalty amount.

This case serves as a clear warning to logistics and freight forwarding companies about the significant sanctions risks associated with dealing in blocked property and the importance of comprehensive, risk-based screening beyond just names, as well as the necessity of fully complying with OFAC subpoenas.

articles.headline: Individual Settles with OFAC for $1,427,230 in Sanctions Violations
body: An individual has agreed to pay $1,427,230 to settle potential civil liability for apparent violations of U.S. sanctions regulations, as announced by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC). The enforcement action highlights OFAC's continued focus on individual accountability for sanctions breaches.

The specific nature of the violations and the sanctions programs involved were detailed in OFAC's enforcement release. Such cases often involve individuals engaging in prohibited transactions with sanctioned countries, entities, or persons, either directly or indirectly.
This settlement underscores the importance for all U.S. persons, regardless of their professional capacity, to understand and comply with OFAC regulations to avoid significant penalties.

articles.headline: Rice Lake Weighing Systems, Inc. Fined $60,764 for Iran Sanctions Violations
body: Rice Lake Weighing Systems, Inc., a Wisconsin-based manufacturer, has agreed to pay $60,764 to settle eight apparent violations of U.S. sanctions on Iran. The violations occurred when its Italian subsidiary, Dini Argeo S.r.l., exported weighing equipment to Iran through a distributor in the United Arab Emirates (UAE), despite knowing the ultimate destination.

The violations took place between July 2019 and November 2021, after the U.S. withdrew from the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action and General License H, which had authorized such transactions, was revoked. OFAC determined the violations were non-egregious and voluntarily self-disclosed.

This case emphasizes that U.S. companies are responsible for ensuring their foreign subsidiaries comply with U.S. sanctions, and that indirect sales through third countries to sanctioned destinations can still lead to significant penalties.

articles.headline: FTI Consulting, Inc. Settles with OFAC for $1,050,000
body: FTI Consulting, Inc., a global business advisory firm, has agreed to pay $1,050,000 to settle its potential civil liability for apparent violations of U.S. sanctions regulations. The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the settlement, which addresses transactions that contravened various sanctions programs.

The enforcement release from OFAC typically details the nature of the violations, including the specific sanctions programs implicated and the circumstances surrounding the prohibited transactions. Such settlements often involve a combination of aggravating and mitigating factors that influence the final penalty amount.

This action serves as a reminder to professional services firms with international operations of the critical importance of implementing and maintaining robust sanctions compliance controls to prevent inadvertent dealings with sanctioned parties or jurisdictions.

articles.headline: Adani Enterprises Limited Pays $275,000,000 in OFAC Settlement
body: Adani Enterprises Limited, a major Indian multinational conglomerate, has agreed to pay a substantial penalty of $275,000,000 to settle potential civil liability for apparent violations of U.S. sanctions regulations. The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced this significant settlement.

While the specific details of the violations are outlined in OFAC's enforcement release, such a large penalty typically indicates a serious breach of sanctions compliance, potentially involving numerous transactions or significant economic benefit to sanctioned parties.

This enforcement action underscores OFAC's global reach and its commitment to enforcing U.S. sanctions against foreign entities, even those in allied nations, when violations occur. It highlights the necessity for all international businesses to rigorously adhere to U.S. sanctions laws.

articles.headline: TradeStation Securities, Inc. Settles with OFAC for $1,110,661
body: TradeStation Securities, Inc., a U.S.-based online brokerage firm, has agreed to pay $1,110,661 to settle its potential civil liability for apparent violations of U.S. sanctions regulations. The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the settlement, addressing transactions that contravened various sanctions programs.

The enforcement release from OFAC typically provides details on the nature of the violations, including the specific sanctions programs implicated and the circumstances surrounding the prohibited transactions. Financial institutions are expected to have robust compliance programs to prevent such breaches.

This action serves as a reminder to financial services companies of their obligations to implement effective sanctions screening and compliance controls to avoid facilitating transactions with sanctioned individuals, entities, or jurisdictions.

articles.headline: Individual Pays $3,777,000 to OFAC for Syrian Sanctions Violations
body: A U.S. citizen residing abroad has agreed to pay $3,777,000 to settle liability for 20 apparent violations of the Syrian Sanctions Regulations. The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the settlement, highlighting its enforcement against individuals who breach sanctions.

The violations occurred between 2018 and 2021, involving transactions that contravened the prohibitions under the Syrian sanctions program. This case underscores OFAC's ability to pursue enforcement actions against individuals, not just corporations, for sanctions non-compliance.
The significant penalty reflects the seriousness of the violations and OFAC's commitment to deterring U.S. persons from engaging in unauthorized activities with sanctioned jurisdictions.

articles.headline: IMG Academy, LLC Settles with OFAC for $1,720,000 Over Kingpin Act Violations
body: IMG Academy, LLC, a U.S.-based academic and athletic training institution, has agreed to pay $1,720,000 to settle apparent violations of the Foreign Narcotics Kingpin Sanctions Regulations. The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the settlement, which stemmed from the academy's enrollment of students whose parents were designated under the Kingpin Act.

Over a five-year period, IMG Academy entered into tuition enrollment agreements with two individuals designated under the Kingpin Act and processed 89 related financial transactions. OFAC found that routine due diligence, such as screening contracting parties or payors, would have revealed that the individuals' names matched entries on the SDN List.

This case serves as a warning to academic institutions, particularly those with international student bodies, that they face significant sanctions exposure and must implement effective, risk-based controls, screening procedures, and training programs to avoid violations.

articles.headline: Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors
body: In this interim final rule (IFR), the Department of Commerce is establishing new rules to prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on U.S. technology to threaten U.S. national security and foreign policy interests. First, this rule establishes new restrictions which will apply for exports, reexports, or transfers (in-country) to overseas data centers that remotely supply significant volumes of compute to companies headquartered in Country Group D:5 or Macau. These restrictions will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using U.S. advanced Super Intelligence (SI) semiconductors to train advanced SI models. Data centers, foreign foundries, and chip exporters are required to perform robust due diligence on their customers, including any direct or indirect ownership or control by persons in Country Group D:5 or Macau, as part of complying with this new control. The license requirement will not apply to commercial recommender systems, such as those used by online retailers or social media companies, as these functions do not pose the same national security threat. Second, in addition to the current license requirements for advanced semiconductors, a license will be required to export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil (and any additional country designated by the Secretary of Commerce, in consultation with the Secretary of State or the Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs)--countries which present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion. The license requirement for these five countries will not apply to semiconductors destined to companies headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent company is headquartered in, the United States, provided certain reporting requirements are met. Commerce will be actively monitoring for countries that tolerate evasion of this IFR and will consider a range of consequences for such countries, such as import restrictions, new license requirements on advanced semiconductor exports, downgrading the country's status in the U.S. export control regime, and Entity List designations and temporary export prohibitions for foreign persons involved in such activities. Third, this IFR amends the presumptions which front-end chips fabricators and chip packagers face when exporting advanced-node logic chips. These amendments reduce the number of pathways to overcome the presumptions for chip designers located in destinations which face a license requirement for SI chips. This change gives the U.S. government critical oversight over companies headquartered in certain countries that seek to leverage advanced semiconductor production capabilities in third countries. Finally, the IFR formally rescinds the regulations implementing the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule. The AI Diffusion Rule has never been enforced. The regulatory changes in this rule formalize the rescission of the AI Diffusion Rule, which the Department of Commerce Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced in May 2025.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.
